Indian PM Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit that will begin on Saturday.

The two leaders "exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral sphere, in particular in BRICS under India’s Chairship for 2026," a statement by India's Ministry of External Affairs said.

In the meeting, the leaders also exchanged views on "key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers."

articles.title: Saudi airstrikes hit Yemen's rebel-held Mokha airport as Houthis capture strategic island
articles.summary: Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured a strategic island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the entrance of the Red Sea, two officials said Friday, in a swift advance that further threatens Saudi…

image.caption: Yemen's Houthi rebels march during a mobilization campaign in Sanaa, Yemen on Thursday. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured a strategic island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the entrance of the Red Sea, two officials said Friday, in a swift advance that further threatens Saudi oil exports through one of the world's key commercial lanes.
Houthis' advance threatens critical shipping alternative to Strait of Hormuz

Saudi Arabia responded with airstrikes against the airport in the key port city of Mokha that the Houthis seized on Thursday, a Houthi broadcaster said. There was no immediate report of damage or deaths.

The capture of Mayun, a tiny, barren volcanic island in the strait, was confirmed by a senior military official with Yemen's internationally recognized government and by a Houthi official. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to journalists.
The island, also known as Perim, is about 3.5 kilometres off Yemen's west coast.

The strait is a key alternative to the Iran-choked Strait of Hormuz, which has been impacted by the ongoing Iran war. But there is "no need for international concern," Hazam al-Assad, a member of the rebels' political bureau, told The Associated Press, saying they are responding to Saudi aggression, and "our forces have a bank of big important targets" in case Riyadh keeps up the strikes.

Earlier Friday, Iran's government called for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen, throwing its support behind its ally, the Houthis. In its first statement since the rebels entered the port, Iran's Foreign Ministry also called for a return to negotiations between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
There was no immediate Saudi comment on Friday.

items: Iran-backed Houthis attack Saudi oil facilities, injuring dozens
Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Aramco oil facility in Saudi Arabia

blocks.text: The rebels' capture of Mokha, overlooking tanker routes out of the Red Sea, could boost Iran's strategy of driving up world oil and gas prices to pressure the United States, according to experts. It also raises concerns of a new front opening after more than six months of war in the region — one in which Saudi Arabia is forced to respond.

Experts say the developments in Yemen could give Tehran more leverage in any negotiations with the U.S. On Wednesday, the spokesperson for Iran's Revolutionary Guard called for any negotiated settlement with the U.S. to include Yemen, the first explicit reference to that front.
Advance threatens key Strait of Hormuz alternative

The Houthis' entry into Mokha on Thursday was their biggest territorial gain in years against their Saudi-backed Yemeni opponents. It brought them within 80 kilometres of the Bab el-Mandeb, a strait that has become an important alternative for global shipping as Iran targets vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

A senior military official with Yemen's internationally recognized government told the AP they were stunned that the Saudi air force didn't strike the Houthis earlier, as they were advancing on Mokha. He assessed that Saudi Arabia didn't get a green light from the U.S. to embark on a large-scale air campaign.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't allowed to speak to the media, also blamed "lack of coordination" between Yemen's army and allied forces, saying it gave the Houthis "a priceless opportunity."

The Houthis had already attacked Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb and Red Sea since declaring a blockade there in July, as well as oil infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said it was in response to the kingdom's blockade of Houthi-held parts of Yemen, in place for years.
Global shipping fears widen as Iran-backed Houthis claim strikes on 2 Saudi oil tankers

New disruption to the waterway could mean trouble for all shipping and for the price of crude oil, which has now soared again. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. About 12 per cent of the world's goods are typically shipped through the strait.

Shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb had fallen by about 60 per cent since the Houthis began attacking some ships there in late 2023 while expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. Shipping increased this year as Saudi Arabia sought alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, but renewed Houthi threats have "curtailed" that activity, according to maritime data and intelligence company Lloyd's List Intelligence.

Saudi Arabia, which earlier this week said it had always offered "opportunities for negotiation," also has said it has the right to defend itself in response to the Houthis' blockade. The foreign ministers of Iran and Saudi Arabia spoke Thursday about diplomatic efforts to "restore stability" to the region, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on social media.
Fighting risks return to civil war
In a statement released Friday, the National Defence Council of Yemen's Saudi-backed and internationally recognized government strongly condemned the Houthis' renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The council also acknowledged that Yemen's government is on the front line of freedom of navigation, and called for international support as the Houthis swept along the Red Sea coast toward the Bab el-Mandeb.
The escalating fighting threatens to end a fragile truce that had largely halted Yemen's civil war since 2022.
At stake are the 40 million people in the Arab world's poorest country who fear a return to the conflict that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.

The surge in fighting in the past week has sent over 46,000 people fleeing, and "overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mokha with their belongings," the UN migration agency said Friday

The Houthis have been at war with Yemen's government since 2014, when the rebels swept from their mountainous heartland and seized much of northern and central Yemen, and the capital of Sanaa. Saudi Arabia entered the war the following year on behalf of the government.

articles.title: Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones
articles.summary: Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity

blocks.text: Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity.
At least two people were killed and six injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital.

At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northern Kyiv, bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car . The blown out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood.
Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later said Russia had carried out a double-tap attack on the facility.

“This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station. “It feels like life is on the edge”.
All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company.

Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting head of Naftogaz, Ukrnafta’s parent company, said: “There is, and can be, no military objective behind such attacks. This is terror directed at the civilian population, at peaceful people.”
after newsletter promotion
A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. . The three struck so far were on the list.

At the other station hit on Friday, in Desnianskyi district, one of the most densely populated parts of the capital, the manager of a nearby car wash said it had been a miracle that no one had died in the blast.

Fedir Lesovin, said the air-raid siren had given the petrol station workers time to run to a nearby shelter, and that a customer waiting outside his business saw the incoming drone and also ran to safety.

Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian petrol stations in recent months. Facilities in the east and south of the country have been repeatedly targeted, but this week’s attacks mark the first time that strikes against a vital part of daily life have been brought to the capital.
Ukraine has also targeted Russian oil infrastructure. Its special forces said this week that they had struck facilities at the Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala.

Kyiv has been pounded by daily drone and missile strikes since late August, at a time when Ukraine is running low on Patriot interceptors. A brief reprieve for the visit of the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff over the weekend ended on Monday.

The petrol station attacks happened as Volodymyr Zelenskyy was on an overseas trip intended to drum up international support and aid before what is expected to be a difficult winter. . On Thursday the Ukrainian president met Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, who offered support to help boost Ukraine’s drone stocks.
Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

articles.title: How Ron DeSantis politicized Florida’s higher education by placing his loyalists at the top
articles.summary:
Term-limited, hard-right governor instituted an ideological infiltration of universities by placing allies in powerful posts

In fewer than four months’ time, Ron DeSantis, Florida’s…

blocks.text: In fewer than four months’ time, Ron DeSantis, Florida’s hard-right governor, will be termed out of office, and what critics saw as his relentless eight-year, “anti-woke” assault on higher education in the state will finally be over.

But while DeSantis himself will be gone, numerous hand-picked loyalists will remain in positions of power to protect his ideological makeover of universities and colleges. The latest, Alex Kelly, the governor’s former deputy chief of staff, and Florida commerce secretary, was named last week as the sole finalist in Pensacola state college’s search for a new president, at least the 12th close DeSantis ally to win such a plum post.

If he is paid the same salary as Edward Meadows, the college’s outgoing president, Kelly’s earnings will soar from $186,000 at the commerce department to more than $353,000, according to the Miami Herald.

DeSantis’s two terms were marked at regular intervals with unprecedented attacks on the established order, notably his “hostile takeover” of New College, the former liberal arts college; a push to end campus diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs and stifle free speech, struck down in July by a federal judge.
There was also a steady drum beat of conservative Republican acolytes placed controversially in key university leadership roles, many with no previous experience of higher education administration.

They include Jeanette Nunez, DeSantis’s former lieutenant governor, installed despite protests at Florida International University; and Marva Johnson, a lobbyist, businesswoman and tight political ally nicknamed “Maga Marva”, who last year became president of Florida A&M, the state’s largest historically Black public university, over fierce objection from students, faculty, alumni and four board trustees.

Republican former state representatives Mel Ponder, Tommy Gregory, Fred Hawkins and John Temple all secured lucrative presidencies at state colleges; as did three of DeSantis’s former education commissioners, Anastasios Kamoutsas, Manny Diaz and Richard Corcoran.

All were selected by university boards of trustees and confirmed by the state university system’s board of governors, a 17-member panel of which 14 are direct DeSantis appointees. Ray Rodrigues, chancellor of the state system, is another long-serving Republican politician.

William Johnson, Florida director of PEN America, the free expression advocacy group that has challenged many of DeSantis’s policy changes and political maneuvers, said his administration had “made public education an apparatus of the state”.
He said: “Political influence over higher education isn’t new. Rick Scott [DeSantis’s predecessor] did something similar, but the difference is the scale and the explicit ideological goals behind it.

“It’s been this gigantic sea change on how higher ed is run. One of the key differences between DeSantis and everyone else is basically that you know these appointments have no experience in higher ed, so we can infer their main skill set is simply to follow the administration’s ideological mandates.

“I can’t speak to the cronyism aspects. What I am interested in is cross-checking how many folks have come from any kind of higher ed background and understanding of academic freedom and has that ever been the focus of any of his appointees?
“That’s what I’m curious about. And I would imagine that the answer is very few, if any.”

Amanda Phalin, an associate professor in the University of Florida’s school of business, experienced first-hand the state’s approach to university hires as a faculty representative (not appointed by the governor) on the state board from 2023 to 2025.

She remains outraged by its rejection of Santa Ono, an experienced academic chosen as UF president last year by the university’s own trustees, after his earlier advocacy for DEI initiatives came to light.
“My position and opinion about the state university system changed pretty dramatically after the despicable and borderline insane treatment of Dr Ono by the board of governors,” she said.
“You had members of the board of governors who were going against the choice of the board of trustees. They were all DeSantis appointees, but they were having sort of an internal squabble.

“The two years I worked on the board of governors, I approached everything in 100% good faith. I had, and still have, strong political disagreements with folks, but I did my best to take them at their word, hear their concerns and really try to work with them constructively and productively.

“What I saw during the whole Santa Ono debacle is that these people do not actually have the best interest of the state university system at heart. For them, the project is either ideological, or about personal power, or both.”

DeSantis has never made a secret of his desire to impose his Florida “blueprint” nationally, and his legacy, Phalin said, could ultimately become other red states following his lead in injecting more politics and dollars into higher education, and tightening their grip on how it is run by appointing faithful followers to key roles.

“The way the state university system of Florida is structured is that each university has a board of trustees, the governor controls who’s on those boards of trustees, and the boards of trustees ultimately answer to the board of governors, and the governor also controls everyone on the board of governors, except the student representative and faculty representative,” she said.

“So it’s not even about the presidencies. That is almost beside the point. What DeSantis has really done is, in a behind-the-scenes structural way, politicized the entire system, top to bottom, in terms of its governance structure.”

articles.title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route
articles.summary: Rampant Yemeni rebels take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports

blocks.text: Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured a strategic island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.

The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.

The Bab al-Mandab links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.

blocks.caption: Fighters loyal to the Houthi authorities march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.

Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied ever since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.

British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.

The surge in fighting in the past week has sent over 46,000 people fleeing, and “overnight, large numbers of people were reportedly seen leaving Mocha with their belongings”, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

blocks.caption: Perim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph. Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./AP

blocks.text: The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.

The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, a blockade that is severely damaging the Iranian economy.

The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.

On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.

Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, leader of the National Resistance forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.

On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel prize winner Tawakkol Karman called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial of charges of conspiracy and high treason.
Saudi Arabia is now facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.

Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.

There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

articles.title: Adiong questions VP Sara's motive in urging PBBM to resign
articles.summary: MANILA – House prosecution panel spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong of Lanao del Sur on Friday questioned Vice President Sara Duterte’s call for President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to resign, noting…

blocks.text: MANILA – House prosecution panel spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong of Lanao del Sur on Friday questioned Vice President Sara Duterte’s call for President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to resign, noting that she would be next in line to benefit from his departure.

In a press briefing, Alonto Adiong said there is a clear conflict of interest in the Vice President’s call, stressing that the public should consider the identity and position of the person making the call, as well as the message itself.

“Una, importante po, hindi lang ang message kundi sino ang nagsasabi ng message na ito (First, and most importantly, it is not just the message itself that matters, but who is delivering it),” Alonto Adiong said.

Duterte called on Marcos to step down after appearing at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, which deferred her arraignment in the grave-threats case at her camp’s request. Addressing supporters, she accused Marcos of dishonesty and abuse.

The Vice President claimed that she could not remain silent while Filipinos struggled with flooding and providing for their families. She urged supporters to continue opposing what she described as abuse and corruption.
Adiong said that people should ask be asking “who stands to benefit” from the Vice President’s call.
Former Surigao del Norte Rep. Ace Barbers, the House prosecution team’s adviser and spokesperson, acknowledged Duterte’s right to express her views about Marcos and the situation she faced.

“Well, karapatan naman niya magsalita o magbigay ng statement kung anong kanyang opinion at nararamdaman (she has the right to speak or issue a statement regarding her opinion and feelings) against anyone and against the situation she’s facing,” Barbers said.
Barbers also pointed to the court proceedings as evidence that Duterte was being given an opportunity to exercise her rights.
“Itong nangyayari ngayon ay patunay na may binibigay na due process para sa kanya (What is happening right now is proof that due process is being accorded to her),” he said.

The Quezon City court directed the Department of Justice to comment on the defense motion before ruling on it. Duterte’s lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, declined to disclose the motion’s contents. The deferral postponed the reading of the charges and entry of a plea.
Barbers said the process should be respected even as Duterte voiced sharply worded criticism.
“She can say whatever she wants to say,” he added. (PNA)

articles.title: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
articles.summary: The Houthi takeovers of Mokha, Dhubab and Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threaten to push Yemen deeper into the Middle East war. The Iran-backed group has made advances against Yemen's government…

image.caption: Yemen's Houthi rebels are seizing strategic towns near the key waterway Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Will Yemen be pulled into the wider US-Iran war?Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen's internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States.
The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces.

The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran's. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces.

"This is actually a full-scale war," Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "It hasn't been given that name yet but we are marching there full time," Al-Muslimi said.
Houthis 'much stronger'

The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen's government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split.

The Houthis control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and most of the country's north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen's joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January.

Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. "The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger," Manea said, "while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented."

blocks.caption: The Houthis targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and said Riyadh retaliated across four provinces in YemenImage: Al Masirah/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's Pakistan's role?

Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen's ousted government. "Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it," Manea said.

The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position.
"At present, I consider the second scenario more likely," Manea said.
Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: "The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost."

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came.

Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. "But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out," Gower said. "Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran," she added, "and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation."

blocks.caption: Thousands of civilians fled their homes this week, while nearly 200 were killed in the fighting, according to international bodiesImage: AFP

blocks.text: Humanitarian toll rises
Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the "harsh reality" of a return to war.

The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen's conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence.

The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warnedthat around 18,500 people have been displaced. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's chief of mission, said in a statement. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before," he said. "Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild."

This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. "When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost," she said.

"Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life," she said. "The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war," she added.

articles.title: Seeing the many things ube can become at Ube Fest
articles.summary: Ube candles, ube scents, and ube art, anyone?

blocks.text: Ube candles, ube scents, and ube art, anyone?
Think you know every way to enjoy ube? Well, Ube Fest proved otherwise.
Held from September 5 to 6 at The Corner House in San Juan, the festival brought together small businesses with their own creative takes on everyone’s favorite purple ingredient.

Some stayed close to ube’s OG dessert roots, while others treated it as a starting point — playing with its color, texture, and aroma in many unconventional ways. The result was part food festival, part small-business showcase, and part answer to the question: How many things can ube become?
Ube may have long been a staple of Filipino desserts, but at Ube Fest, it also found its way into fragrance and art.
Moods & Aroma turned ube into a scented candle, bringing its familiar scent into something for the home.

blocks.caption: UBE GETS LIT — LITERALLY! Moods & Aroma turns ube into scents for your home

blocks.text: Sumi Inklings explored another side of the purple yam by using ube as paint to create art. The artist made the ingredient part of the artwork itself, using its natural color and texture as a creative medium.

blocks.caption: UBE ART. Sumi Inklings trades conventional paint for ube, using the purple yam’s natural color to create one-of-a-kind marbled art. Instagram video screenshot from @sumi.inklings

blocks.text: It was a playful (and really cool) way to look at something usually meant to be eaten. In the hands of an artist, ube’s rich purple color became pigment on the canvas.
But not every product at the fest took ube somewhere uncharted. Some of the most interesting finds simply added it to food Filipinos already know and love.
Ube Taho combined two nostalgic flavors in one cup. Instead of the usual arnibal (brown sugar syrup), ube’s earthy sweetness became an exciting addition to the warm, silken taho.

blocks.caption: UBE TAHO. Bringing an incredible spin on the classic street food staple

blocks.text: Then there was the ube scoopie, an indulgent take featuring warm ube cake topped à la mode with vanilla ice cream. The contrast of warm cake and cold ice cream, dense crumb and creamy melt, made each spoonful especially satisfying.

blocks.caption: UBE SCOOPIE FROM SCOOPA.PH. Moist ube cake topped with melty chocolate and a scoop of vanilla ice cream

blocks.text: Behind Ube Fest were young entrepreneurs Chelsea Yap, Tyrone Tan, and Chloe Sy. The festival gave the three friends a way to enter the events space while building a community around other like-minded peers.
“We wanted to try something unique because a lot of bazaars nowadays revolve around the same themes. We wanted to make connections, make friends, and help other small businesses,” Chelsea said.

To her, ube also presented an opportunity to spotlight a familiar Filipino ingredient through fresh ideas. “It’s such a simple ingredient that can be incorporated into so many different foods and forms. We hope to highlight the unique flavors and food the Philippines has to offer.”

Ube Fest brought a glimpse of that creativity at work. Give local makers one ingredient, and they will find new ways to serve it, scent it, shape it, and build a whole festival around it. The fun was seeing how far they could take ube without losing what people already love about it. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Legarda, son case ‘clearly political persecution’ — spox
articles.summary: The case involving Sen. Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Legarda Leviste is being driven by politics rather than evidence, according to their spokesperson Atty. Tony La…

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 7:50pm
Loren Legarda speaks as a senator-judge in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — The case involving Sen. Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Legarda Leviste is being driven by politics rather than evidence, according to their spokesperson lawyer Tony La Viña.
La Viña said a review of the allegations found no illegal or improper acts by Legarda or Leviste in connection with Leviste's solar energy businesses.
"After intensive review, I am convinced that she and her son have absolutely not done anything illegal and even improper with respect to the solar energy business of the latter," he said.
He stressed that the matter remains at the preliminary investigation stage and that no formal charges have been filed against Legarda or Leviste.

La Viña also rejected attempts to link Legarda to her son's companies, saying there are no corporate documents showing that the senator is a shareholder, officer or beneficiary of Solar Para sa Bayan Corporation or any Solar Philippines company.
"Responsibility is personal," he said. "Senator Legarda should not be shielded from scrutiny because Leviste is her son. But neither should motherhood become evidence against her."

On the congressional franchise granted to Solar Para sa Bayan, La Viña said it was non-exclusive, did not provide government subsidies and depended partly on regulatory action from the Department of Energy. He also noted that Legarda did not vote for its passage.
La Viña said the franchise was never sold and could not be fully implemented because the DOE did not issue the required implementing rules or identify the areas where it could operate.
He also defended Leviste's business ventures, saying entrepreneurial innovation and unsuccessful implementation of an idea should not be treated as criminal conduct.

"Leandro introduced new ideas and approaches to fast-track the energy transition, and there may have been policy gaps that prevented the successful implementation of some of those ideas. But that is not a criminal act," La Viña said.
He claimed that scrutiny of Leviste's projects intensified after the lawmaker publicly exposed alleged corruption in late 2025 and called for investigations.
"The timing speaks for itself," La Viña said, describing the pattern as "classic lawfare, the weaponization of the law for political purposes."
"What is going on is clearly political persecution," he said. "It has always been wrong. And it must stop now."

articles.title: Prosecution team backs ex-SC justices' role in voting threshold debate
articles.summary: House impeachment spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said that the amici curiae have "credibility, expertise, and integrity. So these are perfect experts who have been chosen by the Senate to be…

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 7:49pm
Spokespersons of the House impeachment team welcomed the participation of legal luminaries in the discussion on the conviction voting threshold in the Duterte impeachment trial.

Retired Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban, retired SC Chief Justice Reynato Puno, retired SC Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna, and retired SC Chief Justice Hilario Davide were already named by the Senate impeachment court.

House impeachment spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said in a press conference that the amici curiae have "credibility, expertise, and integrity. So these are perfect experts who have been chosen by the Senate to be part of this process by soliciting their opinions regarding the threshold."

"They have served as former justices of the Supreme Court or chief justices of the Supreme Court. Dalawa po diyan also sat in the Constitutional Convention of 1986 that drafted the 1987 Philippine Constitution," Alonto Adiong added.
Alonto Adiong also said part of the discussion will be "what happened or what transpired during the discussion in the 1986 Constitutional Convention deliberation."
"Baka din po masabi po nila kung ano talaga yung intention, paano nila napag-usapan ito during the deliberation of the framing of the Constitution," he explained.

When asked what the House prosecution panel's stand on the voting threshold is, Alonto Adiong replied, "If you are asking us kung ano yung interpretation natin whether dapat ibaba o dapat remain, yes, there's no official kasi there's no official stand. But ang stand po ng prosecution panel is very clear - we do not engage in vote counting."
House impeachment adviser and spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers believes it is important to consult legal experts on the voting threshold.

"Ako, personally, I subscribe to that kasi mahalaga na magkaroon ng opinion na maaring gawing basehan ng ating impeachment court sa kanilang magiging decision in the future," Barbers said in a press conference.
Barbers said there are differing opinions on what the voting threshold should be and the amici curiae "can give their opinion on the issues."

"Isa diyan sa lumalabas na opinion, it is not fair for a senator-judge to render a decision when he has not seen the evidence, not heard the testimonies of the witnesses, or has not seen the demeanor of the witnesses being presented by both panels," Barbers cited.

"Very important aspect of this trial is when the judges, the senator-judges, will render their decision in this unique situation that we have na kung saan ay marami sa mga senator-judges ay hindi nakapag-participate. Maraming schools of thought na lumalabas," he added.
Whatever the Senate impeachment court decides, Barbers said the issue can still be raised before the Supreme Court.

"The issue can, will just be raised before the Supreme Court if there is already a controversy. I think the objective of this amicus curiae is to get some opinions before the court, as a whole, will decide on whether they will lower down the threshold that would go against the constitutional provision of the concurrence of two-thirds of all members," he explained.

"Ako, personally, ang tingin ko diyan is that though the Senate has the exclusive mandate to try and decide impeachment complaints, when it comes to constitutional provision, it's the Supreme Court that has that mandate to interpret that," Alonto Adiong stated.
The oral arguments on the voting threshold are scheduled for September 23. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte calls Martin Romualdez's arrest 'drama'; Jonvic Remulla says he's stating facts
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday called the arrest of former Speaker Martin Romualdez "drama" days after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that her camp wanted her detained and handcuffed…

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 7:42pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday called the arrest of former Speaker Martin Romualdez "drama" days after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that her camp wanted her detained and handcuffed for dramatic purposes after a Quezon City court ordered her arrest for grave threats.
Asked for comment about Remulla's remarks, Duterte said it was the Interior Secretary who wanted drama.
“Siya yung may gusto ng drama at saka ang totoong drama kung makikita ninyo ay yung pag-aresto kuno kay Martin Romualdez,” Duterte told reporters.
(He is the one who wants drama, and the real drama, if you notice, is the supposed arrest of Martin Romualdez.)
Remulla earlier said that the Duterte camp initially wanted her to be incarcerated after the Philippine National Police (PNP) served a warrant for her arrest over grave threats.
“Ang drama nila, gusto nilang makulong siya. Hindi kami pumayag. We wanted to go according to the rules of law and to the rules of court,” Remulla said.
(They’re making a drama out of it. They wanted her to be jailed, but we did not allow it. We wanted to follow the rules of law and the rules of the court.)
Remulla shrugged off the vice president's remarks and advised that she focus on more pressing matters.
"I think she has bigger things to mind than me. I'm just doing my job stating the facts. She has an impeachment going on," Remulla said.
"Maybe her energies are better focused on real world problems," he said.
Meanwhile, Romualdez's lawyer Ade Fajardo said he "cannot comment at this time" regarding the vice president's remarks about the arrest of his client.

On September 7, police served an arrest warrant to Romualdez over plunder charges in connection with flood control projects while he was confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: PLDT Home brings fiber connectivity to Camotes Island, opening more digital opportunities for families and communities
articles.summary: PLDT Home has expanded its fiber network to Camotes Island, bringing reliable broadband connectivity to more families and communities across the municipalities of San Francisco, Poro, and Tudela.…

blocks.text: PLDT Home has expanded its fiber network to Camotes Island, bringing reliable broadband connectivity to more families and communities across the municipalities of San Francisco, Poro, and Tudela.

Known for its powdery white-sand beaches, underground caves, and rugged cliff-jumping spots, Camotes Island is often called the “Lost Horizon of the South.” Its laid-back atmosphere and natural attractions make it a popular destination for travelers seeking a quieter tropical escape from crowded tourist hubs.

The expansion is part of PLDT’s ongoing commitment to help bridge the digital divide and to extend reliable connectivity to more communities across the country, including those on Camotes Island in the Visayas.

“Expanding into Camotes Island is about more than extending our network footprint. It is about helping close a connectivity gap that can limit access to opportunities. By bringing reliable fiber connectivity to island communities, PLDT Home is providing families with the digital infrastructure they need to participate more fully in today’s digital economy,” said Menardo “Butch” Jimenez Jr., Chief Operating Officer and Chief Technology Officer, PLDT Inc.
More digital opportunities for Camotes families
Residents may subscribe to the new PLDT Home Fiber Unli All 1499 plan, which offers unlimited fiber internet at speeds up to 200 Mbps.

The plan also includes 63 Cignal channels and HBO Max Standard for entertainment, unlimited landline-to-landline calls and landline-to-mobile calls to five nominated Smart or TNT numbers, and 9GB of Smart mobile data each month. By bringing home internet, entertainment, and mobile connectivity together in one plan, Fiber Unli All 1499 gives families more ways to stay connected while helping them make the smart choice for their household’s everyday digital needs.

The new Smart mobile data inclusion extends the home plan’s value beyond the household. Subscribers can share the 9GB monthly allocation with up to three of their nominated Smart or TNT numbers, giving family members mobile data they can use on the go.

Reliable home internet can help students access educational resources, enable family members to work and communicate from home, and give families easier access to digital services such as online banking, telehealth, government platforms, and e-commerce. It can also support home-based entrepreneurs and local businesses that rely on connectivity to reach customers, promote their products and services, and manage transactions online.

Improved connectivity can also support Camotes Island’s continued development as a tourism destination by helping local businesses and residents promote the island’s natural attractions and local experiences to a wider audience while staying connected with customers, visitors, and communities beyond the island.
Working with local communities

PLDT Home partnered with local government units and community partners in San Francisco, Poro, and Tudela to introduce its fiber services to residents. The rollout includes community visits and information booths at key locations, including the Agora Public Market in San Francisco, the RBC Business Center near Poro Port, and an area beside the Tudela Municipal Hall.

The expansion also supports local employment through community-based sales and service activities. PLDT Home is engaging local agents and partners to assist households interested in applying for fiber connectivity.

Through its continued network expansion, PLDT Home reinforces its commitment to Filipino families and communities. It also underscores the PLDT Group’s broader nation-building mission to connect more Filipinos and extend the benefits of technology to communities beyond major urban centers.

Residents may visit PLDT Home booths and authorized local representatives in San Francisco, Poro, and Tudela to inquire about Fiber Unli All 1499 and check service availability in their residential areas.

articles.title: Marcos Sr's 109th birthday: Son recalls father's leadership lessons
articles.summary: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — “Spending time with him – (and) I never knew it – but he was already teaching me. He was already training me,” President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said as he recalled his late…

blocks.text: SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — “Spending time with him – (and) I never knew it – but he was already teaching me. He was already training me,” President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said as he recalled his late father, former President Ferdinand Edralin Marcos Sr.
The President marked his father’s 109th birthday in Ilocos Norte’s Batac City, where the latter was raised.

Marcos said good leadership requires sacrifice and doing what is right even when it is difficult, as he led the celebration at the Bannawag Shrine in Batac. The province of Ilocos Norte observed Friday as a special nonworking day to mark the memorial for the late president
He said his father’s lessons were not about becoming an important public figure or reaching the heights of political leadership.
Rather, he said, his father taught him values that he would carry into public service.

“Do not take whatever is the easy way out. Do what is right, no matter how difficult it may be,” the President said as he recounted his father’s words, adding, “The most important lesson is about your country and your countrymen. “
Recalling moments with his father, Marcos Jr. shared the latter’s teaching style.

“I look back on my life, and I say, it is remarkable because my father never sat me down and said, ‘The lesson for today is that you must learn this, that, and the other thing.’ Hindi ganoon ang style nung aking ama,” he said.
The President noted that Marcos Sr.’s way was “to teach by example and to teach by leadership.”
National interest first
He said the same principles continue to guide him every day as the country’s leader.
“Because in every decision that we make, we must exercise judgment, put the national interest first, and ask what will best serve the Filipino people,” Marcos Jr. said.

He also said, “Because what we do in service of our people is not for ourselves. It is for the country, it is for the people. And you must always remember that there is no sacrifice too great for your people and for your country.”
Marcos Sr. would be 109 years old if he were alive today, having been born on Sept. 11, 1917.
The President led a wreath-laying ceremony at the Marcos Monument following a Thanksgiving Mass at the Immaculate Conception Parish in Batac, attended by the First Family.
He paid tribute to his father’s years in public service and reflected on the values and principles that he said continue to shape his commitment to serving Filipinos.
Natnateng Cook-Off
The commemoration also included a “Natnateng” (Vegetables) Cook-off at the Imelda Cultural Center, featuring vegetable dishes from the province and celebrating Ilocos Norte’s agricultural traditions.
The event came two days before Marcos Jr.’s 69th birthday on Sept. 13.
The President, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and their children joined the Natnateng Cook-Off.
The First Family toured the food displays and sampled dishes featuring locally grown vegetables and traditional Ilocano flavors.
In a sweet moment during the event, Marcos Jr. gave the First Lady a bite of one featured dish, drawing smiles from those who witnessed the gesture.
The annual Natnateng Cook-Off brought together 19 municipalities and two cities to showcase creative dishes made from local vegetables and other indigenous ingredients.

The featured dishes included Ti Hardin ni Nana Maria, Marungay Baraniw Pasta, Binungon nga Pinakbet, Garbage Roll, Breadfruit, Pinakbet Lasagna with Squash Purée and Crispy Bagnet Toppings, Curriwow Seafood Stuffed Vegetables, Dinengdeng: Uong, Sabong, Bulong, and Gastronomic Veggie Longganisa.

The President was also set to be serenaded with “Padapadakam,” a traditional Ilocano birthday song, and receive flowers from members of his family and local officials. ? with Kenneth Tabin, contributor

articles.summary: Prosecutors say the suspects had moved beyond general preparations and were already pursuing a concrete plan for a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets.

image.caption: German federal prosecutors have charged seven suspected Hamas members over an alleged plotImage: Friso Gentsch/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German federal prosecutors on Friday charged seven suspected members of the Islamist militant group Hamas.
The men allegedly plotted to carry out a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets in Germany or Austria.
What are the charges?
The men are accused of helping procure weapons and taking part in preparations for an attack, the Federal Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said on Friday.
Investigators believe the suspects, who were arrested in Germany and abroad over recent months, were already pursuing a concrete attack plan.
The men are accused of helping obtain guns and ammunition for an attack targeting representatives of Israel, Jewish people or people regarded as pro-Israel.
Prosecutors say the plot had become concrete by July 2025 and was intended to take place on the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel.
What weapons had allegedly been obtained?
By the time three of the suspects were arrested in Berlin on October 1, 2025, prosecutors say the group had obtained:

items: one functioning fully automatic rifle
13 functioning handguns
more than 700 rounds of ammunition

blocks.text: Part of the arsenal was allegedly moved to Vienna and stored there by another suspect who is being prosecuted separately.
This is a breaking story that will be updated...

articles.title: Israel says it has destroyed major underground Hezbollah base
articles.summary: The powerful blast registered as the equivalent of a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.

blocks.text: Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.
It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge.
The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.
There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government.

Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March.
Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) showed a fireball lighting up the sky.
"The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC.
"The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake."
He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut.
Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north.

The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives.
"This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram.
"All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled."
The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area.

The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border.
Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district.

The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported.
Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.
Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.
Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.
Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.
Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.

At least 4,362 people have been killed in Lebanon during the conflict, including 395 women and 259 children, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians.
Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed.
Additional reporting by Raffi Berg in London and Samantha Granville and Ghaith Solh in Beirut

articles.title: Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOs
articles.summary:
Human rights organisations concerned about people – including age-disputed children – returned under one in, out out deal

Hundreds of asylum seekers – including at least 41 age-disputed…

blocks.text: Hundreds of asylum seekers – including at least 41 age-disputed children – removed to France under the “one in, one out” deal have disappeared, human rights organisations have said.

The one in, one out pilot scheme was hailed as “groundbreaking” by the former prime minister Keir Starmer when he and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, announced it in July 2025. Under a treaty drawn up for this agreement, it forcibly returns one small-boat asylum seeker to France in exchange for another asylum seeker brought legally to the UK from France.
The deal is due to expire on 1 October and at the moment it is not known what, if anything, will replace it.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is reportedly pushing for the deal to be extended and scaled up, but the French government has indicated that it wants to see the scheme expanded Europewide rather than France having to accept small-boat returnees alone.
One French politician told the Guardian that so far, France’s overtures to other countries to take back a share of small-boat asylum seekers had received a negative response.

blocks.caption: A refugee folds his blanket at a makeshift camp on the outskirts of Calais. Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from the UK to France have disappeared, NGOs report. Photograph: Kiran Ridley/Getty Images

blocks.text: About 1,400 small-boat arrivals have been returned to France since September 2025, just 4% of 32,000 who have crossed the Channel since the deal was signed.

These figures do not include the significant minority who have come back to the UK a second time, some of whom are now living under the radar here. The UK and France amended the treaty to allow for people returning to the UK in lorries to be sent back to France a second time.

At a meeting in parliament this week chaired by Lord German, a general rapporteur on asylum and migration policy for the parliamentary assembly for the Council of Europe, and Alex Sobel, the new chair of parliament’s joint committee on human rights, parliamentarians were told about the disappearances and other concerns about the scheme by NGO representatives working on the ground.

Maddie Harris, the director of the Humans For Rights Network, said several NGOs had between them compiled a list of at least 41 age-disputed children and young people whom they claimed had been unlawfully returned to France. It is unlawful to detain lone children in adult immigration detention centres, and they are excluded from the one in one out treaty.
The Home Office disputed this and told the Guardian: “This is categorically untrue. Nobody has been returned to France where their age is in dispute.

“Every detained person is advised of their right to legal representation and how they can obtain such representation within 24 hours of arrival at an immigration removal centre. Age assessments are carried out to maintain the integrity of our border, while ensuring those genuinely under 18 receive the appropriate support.”

blocks.caption: A screengrab from video issued by the Home Office shows Border Force officers processing small-boat migrants, including biometric and security checks, before their relocation to an immigration removal centre to await their return to France.  Photograph: Home Office/PA

blocks.text: However, the prisons and detention Independent Monitoring Boards have reported that almost a hundred children had been identified as unlawfully detained as adults for the scheme. The IMBs’ interim chair, Jane Leech, attended the meeting and raised concerns that some people were being unlawfully detained for the scheme because the Home Office was “detaining more people than they can remove”.
after newsletter promotion

French politicians have told the Guardian that only 200 people forcibly returned to France were still in contact with the authorities there, with hundreds of others having gone underground in countries across Europe.

The Guardian has interviewed dozens of returnees who are no longer in contact with the French authorities and are living underground in Europe. They say they have disappeared due to hostility from the French authorities, pressure to return to their home countries where they believe they will be unsafe, or the threat of being forced back to other European countries such as Bulgaria that they passed through on their journeys.
Home Office sources said that what happened to people once they were returned to France was a matter for the French authorities. France’s interior ministry declined to comment on the disappearances.

blocks.caption: Border Force officers process small-boat arrivals detained under the one in, one out deal at the Manston immigration centre in Kent. Photograph: Home Office/PA

blocks.text: Harris said the forced return of lone children to France was “shameful”. She said: “We support many children detained under this scheme and attempt to secure their release. However, at least 41 children have been removed from the UK to France and their whereabouts is currently unknown. The vast majority of these children have experienced acute violence and exploitation and are now without protection somewhere in Europe.”

Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, told the parliamentary meeting that asylum seekers were returned to France from the UK in a “deeply concerning” condition, with many displaying severe psychological symptoms such as flashbacks, acute anxiety, self-harm, suicidal thoughts and psychological breakdown.
“What we are witnessing is the accumulation of trauma on trauma,” she said.

Sobel said he was “deeply concerned” about the ongoing securitisation of the French border to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel to the UK. “The French police are doing things it would be unacceptable for British police to do,” he said.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 7:29pm
Authorities declared ‘fire out’ on MV June Aster on Friday, according to the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG).

The official declaration was at 10:15 a.m. on Friday but was only later disclosed to the media. While the PCG has not yet released an updated death tally following the fire being put out, it confirmed that burnt bodies were observed.

“The PCG, PNP-SOCO (Philippine National Police - Scene of the Crime Operations), and other concerned agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures,” PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said in a statement.
“We recognize the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident. Rest assured that operations are carried out with utmost respect for the deceased and their bereaved families,” she added.

blocks.caption: Photo from Philippine Coast Guard

blocks.text: Photo from Philippine Coast Guard
The PCG has laid out oil spill booms as a precautionary measure but said that there were no signs of an oil spill yet in the waters.
In the PCG’s last update, at least 86 people were still missing, and five were dead, with 43 survivors.

blocks.caption: Photo from Philippine Coast Guard

blocks.text: The MV June Aster, owned and operated by Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., caught fire on Wednesday night while it was sailing in the waters of Coron, Palawan. Its flames persisted until Friday morning, making it difficult for rescuers to respond. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: 9/11 conspiracy theories that continue to circulate
articles.summary: A quarter-century after the September 11, 2001, attacks, they are still the focus of numerous conspiracy theories. Why do people believe them?

image.caption: Almost 3,000 people died in the al-Qaeda terrorist attacks against the US on September 11, 2001Image: akg-images GmbH/epd

blocks.text: The terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, also known as 9/11, were the worst such attacks in history. Twenty-five years on, they have been thoroughly investigated and analyzed — yet many people still believe the conspiracy theories that swirl around the suicide attacks in the United States.

First, a reminder of the event itself. On September 11, 2001, the Islamist terrorist network al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger planes. Two were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York City. A third crashed into the Pentagon, just outside Washington, D.C., the headquarters of the US Department of Defense. The fourth airliner is believed to have been heading for the Capitol in Washington, the seat of the US Congress, but it crashed in rural Pennsylvania after passengers staged an intervention to prevent the hijackers from reaching their target. The suicide attackers killed almost 3,000 people that day, and injured thousands more. Live footage of the attacks was broadcast all around the world.
September 11 was an event that changed the world — not only in terms of terrorism, but also conspiracy theories.

"September 11 was a trigger point that led to so many things: debates in society as a whole that hadn't happened before, security problems no one had had to deal with before," historian Claus Oberhauser explained in an interview with fact checkers from BR-Faktenfuchs.

blocks.caption: One passenger plane was flown into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US Department of DefenseImage: StockTrek Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Daniel Jolley is a professor of social psychology at the University of Nottingham who researches the societal repercussions of conspiracy theories. He told DW that conspiracy theories often spring up around events like this. Even today, many people still wonder how it was possible for the most powerful country in the world to be so utterly blindsided — and some believe conspiracy narratives provide the answer.
20% of Americans believe the government was involved

According to a 2023 YouGov survey, one in five Americans believe the US government was behind the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It's a claim that has been circulating for decades. Jolley said it shows that many people mistrust institutions and "those in power."

A conspiracy narrative that bolsters this myth is the claim that the twin towers and other World Trade Center buildings were brought down not by two passenger jets — or not by these alone — but with controlled explosions.

Not only does this allegation continue to spread on social media, it is also based on the assertions of a small number of scientists. For example, one of their arguments is that the horizontal clouds of smoke seen when the towers collapsed supposedly indicate controlled explosions in lower floors.

blocks.caption: Both of the World Trade Center towers collapsed about an hour after they were hit by the planesImage: Louis Lanzano/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, there is no evidence whatsoever that explosives or bombs were found at the site. Investigations like the one carried out by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) explain how the two passenger planes crashing into the twin towers caused them to catch fire and collapse. According to the NIST, videos of the attack support the scientific evidence.
Other analyses, like those done by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) or the consultancy firm Weidlinger Associates, reached the same conclusion.
Why do people believe conspiracy theories?
Events like 9/11 can leave certain psychological needs unfulfilled, Jolley explained: "The needs being: to want to feel in control, to want to feel certain, to want to not feel anxious."
Initially, especially with sudden, expected events like this, there are many unanswered questions and gaps in our knowledge. How did the attack happen? Who was behind it?

"These gaps in our knowledge are precisely what encourage conspiracy theories to spring up," said Oberhauser. And then some people start to entertain the possibility that an even bigger conspiracy is behind it all.
Karen Douglas, a professor of social psychology at the University of Kent, confirmed this. "Anyone can fall into conspiracy theories if the circumstances are right," she told DW.

blocks.caption: The south tower was the first to collapse, as New Yorkers watched in horrorImage: Syndi Pilar/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, Jolley added that it's not the case that a person wakes up one day and suddenly distrusts the world. "Rather, this may have been a journey based on their life experience; for example, the adversities in their life," he said. The way a person generally deals with crises is also relevant. An anxious person is more likely to succumb to conspiracy theories, he added.

Social networks in particular contribute to the rapid spread of myths. Social media already existed before September 11, 2001, but its big breakthrough came with Facebook in 2004. Apps like Instagram, WhatsApp, Telegram and YouTube are now used by billions of people. They're used to share false information and conspiracy narratives, and the platforms don't always act swiftly to take them down.

"They become part of our everyday content, whether it's on our phones, on TikTok, on other social media platforms, where we can kind of come down that rabbit hole very, very quickly," said Jolley. "Going down a rabbit hole" means taking a very intense interest in a subject, clicking from one link to another, and "falling" ever deeper — like Alice in Wonderland.

blocks.caption: Disproved conspiracy theories continue to circulate about various aspects of the 9/11 attacksImage: akg-images GmbH/epd

blocks.text: Why are conspiracy theories problematic?
There are three main reasons why conspiracy theories are so dangerous.

items: Conspiracy narratives hold out the promise of making people feel less anxious and more secure. But as Jolley explained, the opposite is more likely to be the case. This can result in even greater mistrust of the government, and of other people, resulting in social isolation.

A conspiracy theory mixes reality and misinformation; and, unlike disinformation, it cannot easily be exposed as false as it is not based on clear statements that can be verified or disproved. The very essence of a conspiracy theory is the idea that a group of conspirators are acting in secret and the general public are not supposed to know anything about it.

Conspiracy theories have consequences, and can influence how people act, said Douglas. "Conspiracy theories historically have been linked with prejudice, genocide, risky health behavior, climate denial, and more recently some disturbing behavior related to QAnon and COVID-19 conspiracy theories."

blocks.text: One group has been a particular focus of conspiracy theories around 9/11: Jews. The myth that Jewish people were behind the attacks has been widely shared on social media. This claim can be traced to the antisemitic trope that "the Jews" are a collective supposedly seeking world domination or to control the world. There is no evidence whatsoever to support this conspiracy theory, either.

blocks.caption: Today, a memorial to those who died on 9/11 stands on the site of the former World Trade CenterImage: Piotr Kucza/Fotopyk/newspix/IMAGO

blocks.text: According to Jolley, certain groups — including Jews, Muslims and LGBTQ+ people — are often blamed for crimes they did not commit. Throughout history, Jews in particular have often been the focus of conspiracy myths, and this continues to this day. An example from Germany is that of the right-wing extremist who tried to storm a synagogue, then killed two people at a nearby kebab shop in Halle in 2019. He had been sharing antisemitic conspiracy theories online.
How can societies respond to conspiracy narratives?

In Germany, nongovernmental organizations like the Amadeu Antonio Foundation or the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb) give advice on how to deal with friends or family who believe conspiracy theories. For example: Communicate with each other on equal terms, and conduct research together to find reliable information, and call out antisemitism, racism and other extreme positions, and make it clear that you oppose them. The historian Oberhauser stressed that people need to learn to go back to trusting facts and science.
This article, translated from German, was written as part of a collaboration with the ARD public broadcaster's fact-checking network.

articles.title: PAGASA monitors 2 LPAs outside PAR; southwest monsoon weakens
articles.summary: The trough or extension of one of the low pressure areas is causing scattered rain in Northern Luzon on Friday, September 11

blocks.text: FORECAST. PAGASA Weather Specialist Daniel James Villamil explains the bureau's 4 pm forecast for the two low pressure areas outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility on September 11, 2026.
PAGASA
The trough or extension of one of the low pressure areas is causing scattered rain in Northern Luzon on Friday, September 11
MANILA, Philippines – The weather bureau is monitoring two low pressure areas (LPAs) outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).
The first LPA, which formed over the West Philippine Sea on Thursday, September 10, was located 1,005 kilometers west of southwestern Luzon as of 3 pm on Friday, September 11.
It has a medium chance of developing into a tropical depression within 24 hours, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA).
The potential tropical cyclone is less likely to enter PAR as it is expected to move away from the country in the coming days.

But the trough or extension of this LPA is causing scattered rain and thunderstorms in the Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, and Cagayan Valley on Friday. Flash floods and landslides are possible.
Scattered rain and thunderstorms are also being experienced in the rest of Luzon, Western Visayas, and Northern Samar on Friday, but due to the southwest monsoon or habagat.
Overall, however, the southwest monsoon has weakened and it is no longer expected to trigger significant rain.
Meanwhile, the second LPA outside PAR is much farther, at 3,035 kilometers east of Eastern Visayas as of 3 pm on Friday.
This LPA is unlikely to become a tropical depression in the next 24 hours, but it may eventually enter PAR. For now, it has no impact on any part of the country.
PAGASA expects two or three tropical cyclones to develop within or enter PAR in September. The next three local tropical cyclone names are Queenie, Rosal, and Samuel. – Rappler.com
