articles.title: Alas Pilipinas veterans lead new generation at Asian Games
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — From the Philippine women’s volleyball team that competed in the 2018 Asian Games in Indonesia, only Dawn Macandili-Catindig and Jia De Guzman remain in the program, this time…

blocks.text: Alas Pilipinas women huddle during a timeout in the SEA V Cup.–SAVA PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — From the Philippine women’s volleyball team that competed in the 2018 Asian Games in Indonesia, only Dawn Macandili-Catindig and Jia De Guzman remain in the program, this time leading a new generation of national team stars.

Catindig and De Guzman, both Asian Games debutants eight years ago, urged their younger Alas Pilipinas Women teammates to embrace the moment as they return to the Games starting next week in Aichi-Nagoya.

“I think the difference is that back then, we were the young ones,” Catindig said in Filipino. “Now, we’re the ones helping the younger players and figuring out how we can help them prepare mentally, especially when we’re up against bigger teams.
“We just want them to embrace the experience. Win or lose, the experience is really what we hold on to.”

Catindig and De Guzman are guiding Asian Games first-timers Eya Laure, Bella Belen, Alyssa Solomon, Niña Ytang, Angel Canino, Dell Palomata, Erika Santos, Mars Alba, Thea Gagate, Amie Provido and Justine Jazareno.
“We’re just continuing with our preparation and doing our best despite all the challenges,” Catindig said.

The veteran libero said the team has been thriving under Japanese coach Taka Minowa, the husband of Jaja Santiago-Minowa, after winning a historic silver medal in the second leg of the SEA V Cup last month.

“Under Coach Taka, it’s pretty much the same approach, especially when it comes to playing internationally,” Catindig said. “His strategy as a coach is really to strengthen our basic skills, particularly our serve-receive and defense. So that’s what we’ve been working on.”
Alas will face China, which is seeking a third straight Asian Games title, and Kazakhstan in Pool B.
Catindig hopes the Philippines can carry its confidence into its match against Kazakhstan, which Alas defeated in the 2025 AVC Women’s Cup on the way to a runner-up finish.
“We’ve beaten Kazakhstan before, so I think it’s possible for us to do it again,” Catindig said.

“I think what we’ll hold on to is the advantage we have within our own team. We’ll really study our opponents so that even when we face bigger teams, we can still find ways to use our strengths to our advantage.”

articles.title: Comelec: Reports of shaded ballots ahead of BARMM polls false
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) has dismissed reports of volunteers allegedly shading ballots ahead of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) has dismissed reports of volunteers allegedly shading ballots ahead of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary polls scheduled on Sept. 14.

Comelec’s clarification on Friday followed a post by the Facebook page Mapag Matyag, which claimed that municipal employees or teachers in BARMM had shaded ballots three days before the region’s historic polls.

The poll body assured the public that the ballots are secured in the respective offices of the municipal or city treasurer of five provinces in the region, noting that the ballot boxes are vacuum-sealed and will only be opened on the day of the polls.

“It is the duty of the Election Office and/or the Treasurer of each municipality or city to inspect these items after the public, political parties, candidates, and citizens’ arms have been notified, in order to ensure that the ballots arrived securely and that the quantities and labels are correct,” Comelec said.

The poll body also addressed concerns about a major power outage across BARMM that may occur on election day. It assured that the batteries of the Automated Counting Machine can last more than 14 hours.
It urged the public to refrain from sharing unverified information and to rely only on official announcements released by the Comelec and concerned agencies regarding the BARMM elections.
“Any issue found with the delivered ballots must be immediately reported to the Command Center at the Alnor Hotel and Convention Center, Cotabato City,” it said. /mcm

articles.title: Nerve, RappLearn launch crisis management masterclass for the AI age
articles.summary: Join the masterclass to learn how to anticipate, detect, and effectively manage crisis and online threats

blocks.text: What do you do when the story about you or your organization is no longer yours to control?

Generative AI can produce persuasive content at the press of a button. This blurs the line between authentic information and deceptively manipulated information, according to the UN Preliminary Report of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
When your audiences are challenged to distinguish fact from fiction, your organization’s next crisis won’t just move fast — it will move at the speed of AI.

The Nerve understands this high-stakes information environment and how to respond during hard pressed situations. The data forensics company is partnering with RappLearn, Rappler’s training arm, to launch Under Pressure: Managing Crisis in the Age of AI to help organizations proactively navigate the online space. This hands-on workshop will happen in the Rappler Newsroom in Pasig City on Friday, October 9, 2026, from 9 am to 5 pm.

Born from crisis and forged in fire, The Nerve has spent nearly a decade helping corporate and institutional partners manage online threats and understand real-world trends. Through this immersive masterclass, participants will learn directly from the experts to gain the right toolkits to anticipate, detect, and effectively mitigate crisis incidents.
Attendees will practice rapid triage, undergo mock media interviews, and learn to craft their own crisis management playbook.

This masterclass is designed for communication practitioners with a beginner to intermediate level of understanding of reputational crisis and risk. The session is specifically built for teams operating at a reactive or developing stage of crisis resilience, helping them move from “firefighting” to a proactive, framework-driven state including the following groups:

items: Crisis & PR Managers
Brand Marketing Leaders
Media & Information Practitioners
Academic & Public Institutions
Government & Regulatory Agencies
A Customized Crisis Response Blueprint: Walk away with a tailored operational playbook to map your company’s vulnerability, define escalation guidelines, and coordinate swift internal action.
The 5-Step Forensic Framework: Master a step-by-step methodology built by The Nerve to classify risks, locate digital fires, map online networks, decode threats, and reclaim your narrative.
Real-World Media Discipline Under Fire: Face mock interviews with newsroom journalists to practice rapid-fire holding statements and maintain message discipline under extreme pressure.

Strategies Against AI & Coordinated Campaigns: Learn how to identify and classify actors such as bots, micro-influencers and mainstream media, and map strategies to activate trusted allies to defend your company.
Rapid Triage Skills: Gain the instincts to instantly distinguish between minor issues, incidents, and full-blown crises so your team stops reacting out of panic and starts leading with data.

blocks.text: Kit Posadas is Head of Strategy at The Nerve, a data forensics consultancy born from Rappler’s investigative work on disinformation, now enabling changemakers to navigate real-world trends and issues. Her expertise lies in making insights from big data actionable for brands — be it for reputation management, communications planning, or marketing and branding campaigns.

Miriam Grace Go is Managing Editor at Rappler. Gigi is an award-winning investigative journalist and author who has spent decades covering local governance, campaigns, and elections across various publications. Recognized as an outstanding UP alumnus and Glory Medal of Distinction recipient, she has co-authored multiple books on Philippine politics and has completed fellowships in Hawaii, Canada, and Thailand.

Pauline Macaraeg is the Lead Forensics Researcher at The Nerve. Her work focuses on analyzing data-driven online trends, mapping disinformation actors and networks, and decoding the spread of information across the digital space. She has an academic foundation in Data Science through her MS studies at the Asian Institute of Management.

articles.title: Marcos departs for 2-day BRICS Summit in India
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday left Manila to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 7:08pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday left Manila to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.
In his departure message, Marcos said that his travel to India from September 12 to 13, 2026, was at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The President is set to represent the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) community in the BRICS Summit in the Philippines’ capacity as chair of the regional organization for 2026.

“In this role, I will carry ASEAN's voice to the summit and help amplify our community's perspectives on the issues of our time, guided by the priorities of our chairship, peace and security anchors, prosperity corridors, and people empowerment,” Marcos said.

“We will engage the BRICS community, whose ranks include four of our fellow ASEAN member-states, on advancing our quest for peace, inclusive growth, regional resilience, sustainable development, food and energy security, and a rules-based international order,” he added.
During the opening session of the Summit on September 13, Marcos said he will have the opportunity to present the priorities of ASEAN to the BRICS members.

He said he plans to highlight ASEAN’s commitment to deepen its engagement with its partners through established frameworks, and offer views on how partners can and should work to address challenges, especially those that affect developing countries and emerging economies.

“We will call for fairer global governance, stronger disaster preparedness, the responsible use of new technologies, climate action, and the peaceful settlement of disputes under international law. We will bring lessons from ASEAN’s track record and long-standing commitment to open and inclusive dialogue, while preserving strategic autonomy,” the President said.
While in India, Marcos is also set to have a bilateral meeting with Modi.

Marcos said that he and the Indian leader will track progress in the key areas of the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and will review the progress in the implementation of the Five-Year Plan of Action for 2025-2029.

“Our discussions will cover defense and maritime cooperation, trade and investment, the proposed Preferential Trade Agreement, health and pharmaceuticals, digital cooperation, tourism, direct air connectivity, and people-to-people ties,” he said.
He also said he would renew the invitation for Modi to visit the Philippines for the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit in November.
Marcos said he will also engage with Indian companies and players.
“We thus embark for India determined to continue the task of translating potential to action,

and action into gains—gains for greater economic security for the Filipino people, for ASEAN and its external partnerships, and for fostering broader practical cooperation among players, even of differing persuasions, to support peace, security, and shared prosperity,” the chief executive said.

“I look forward to another productive visit to India, to engaging leaders, nations, and entities participating in the BRICS Summit, and to opening more doors for the Philippines and for ASEAN,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Lapu-Lapu City Hospital shuns claims of late care in child’s death
articles.summary: Lapu-Lapu City Hospital has issued a statement addressing allegations of delayed or inadequate care after the death of a child who was brought to its emergency room on September 8, 2026.... Keep on…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — Lapu-Lapu City Hospital has issued a statement addressing allegations of delayed or inadequate care after the death of a child who was brought to its emergency room on Sept. 8, 2026.

The hospital’s statement came after the child’s mother alleged on social media that her child was experiencing difficulty breathing and that the child’s lips had turned bluish or had become “cyanotic,” before hospital staff allegedly moved to discharge the patient instead of admitting or closely monitoring the child.
Mother questions doctor’s decision
The mother said they went to the emergency room around 11 a.m. and waited for the results of an X-ray.

She alleged that a doctor later told her that her child was okay and could be discharged. She questioned the decision, saying the child was already “lagom” (discolored) and having difficulty breathing.
The mother further alleged that her child was only attended to when the condition had already severely worsened.
She said her child continued to struggle to breathe and was eventually difficult to save.
According to her post, the child died around 1:31 a.m.
Hospital’s account
Lapu-Lapu City Hospital said the patient was initially brought to the triage area due to persistent fever and colds before being endorsed to the Emergency Room (ER) shortly afterward.
According to the hospital, the ER physician evaluated the patient, who underwent the necessary diagnostic assessment and was placed on IV fluid hydration and continued observation.
During the patient’s stay, the hospital said the patient developed fever and was given appropriate medication and supportive measures. The patient’s temperature initially improved.
However, the hospital said the patient suddenly developed cyanosis, or “nanglagum ang ngabil,” followed by a generalized seizure and further clinical deterioration.

The patient was initially given oxygen supplementation and nebulization, but the condition continued to worsen, according to the hospital. The patient eventually developed intractable seizures and was intubated.
Despite the resuscitative measures provided, the hospital said the patient’s condition continued to deteriorate.
Case under review

Lapu-Lapu City Hospital said that, based on the medical documentation presently available, the patient was assessed, monitored and managed according to the attending medical team’s clinical judgment and established standards of care.
As of this writing, the hospital said the circumstances surrounding the incident are being carefully reviewed in the interest of transparency, accountability and continuous improvement.
The hospital also appealed to the public to refrain from speculation, sharing unverified information, aggression and intimidation toward its medical staff.
It said the privacy and dignity of the patient and family must be respected, while the safety, security and well-being of healthcare personnel must likewise be protected.

articles.title: Céline Dion fans gather in Paris as singer prepares for sold-out comeback shows
articles.summary:
More than 30,000 due to attend Canadian artist’s opener at Plenitude arena, as thousands without tickets plan Friday night karaoke

More than 30,000 Céline Dion fans have gathered in Paris…

blocks.text: More than 30,000 Céline Dion fans have gathered in Paris for the Canadian singer’s long-awaited return to performing on Saturday night – four years after she revealed her diagnosis of stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological condition.

Thousands more people without tickets have flocked to a series of giant karaoke events across France to belt out Dion’s famous power ballads, in celebration of the star’s health stabilising enough for her to return to the stage.

Paris’s city hall (Hôtel de Ville) organised a free outdoor karaoke for 10,000 people on Friday night as a giant sing-along to hits such as Dion’s My Heart Will Go On, which featured in the Oscar-winning film Titanic and became the second-bestselling single by a woman in music history.

Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, said the capital’s giant street karaoke would honour Dion as “an artist of the people” and a great “unifier” in France. “Music has that singular power to bring together and build a society,” he said.

Dion, who grew up the youngest of 14 children in a small town near Montréal in French-speaking Quebec, has a massive fanbase in France. Her French-language ballads are regularly the most requested songs at karaoke venues.

blocks.caption: Dion performing in Quebec in 2019.  Photograph: Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press/AP

blocks.text: Dion’s popularity also stems from her life story: from an upbringing in a poor Quebec family, singing as a child at her father’s piano bar, to her massive stadium gigs.

Dion, 58, announced in 2022 that she had been diagnosed with the incurable autoimmune disorder, stiff-person syndrome. She took a break from performing, later describing how the condition meant she had suffered muscle spasms so strong that her ribs were broken. She told journalists there were times she could not walk. In the 2024 documentary I Am: Céline Dion she provided insight into the severity of her pain from the condition, including having a seizure.

blocks.caption: Dion with the director Irene Taylor at a special event screening  of I Am: Celine Dion in New York in 2024. Photograph: Andrew Kelly/Reuters

blocks.text: The content of Dion’s series of concerts at the Plenitude arena in La Défense, west of Paris – the biggest indoor concert venue in Europe – have been kept secret. The singer told fans outside her hotel that she was being careful to protect her health, travelling to and from her hotel only to rehearse and greeting waiting fans from a safe distance.

blocks.caption: Dion greeting fans outside her hotel in Paris last week. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Dion told the crowd that the concerts would be longer than her usual performances and advised them to wear comfortable shoes.

Usually in France, Dion would sing a set mostly made up of her French-language hits – her 1995 album D’eux became the biggest-selling Francophone album of all time. But with Paris currently her only venue, many fans are coming from North America and across the world, so English-language hits will also feature.
In April, about 9 million people had registered for the pre-sale ticket lottery. The concerts swiftly sold out.

The Paris region expects the 16-date residence in September and October as well as further sold-out dates in May to boost to the local economy by up to €800m. The Céline Dion frenzy could eclipse the profits seen by local hotels, restaurants and tourist sites around previous concerts by Taylor Swift and Beyoncé.
At the Galeries Lafayette department store, a Céline Dion merchandise corner had seen a steady trade, with some fans arriving before opening hours.

blocks.caption: The Eiffel Tower illuminated for Celine Dion in March 2026, when the comeback concerts were announced. Photograph: Pierre Suu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Alexandra, 36, a civil servant from the Paris region, had bought a T-shirt and signature Céline Dion macarons. “It’s important to me because I grew up with her music,” she said. “My mother was huge a fan so I listened to Céline Dion songs on the way to school.
“Whenever we went on holiday, Céline Dion would be playing in the car. Her music is part of some of my best memories of childhood. She is humble and she has managed to stay very close to the people.”

She added: “I’ve followed her health challenges. I thought she might not be able to perform again. But she has clearly set herself an incredible challenge and I hope she can manage these concerts without impacting her health. I think she’ll be so lifted up by the fans’ love for her that she will find strength in it.”

articles.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
articles.summary: The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Putin and Xi are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?

image.caption: This year's BRICS host India has to balance welcoming new members like Iran without appearing to snub the USImage: Qamar Sibtain/IANS

blocks.text: In preparation for hosting the 18th BRICS summit in Delhi this weekend, India came up with a slogan which tried to keep the group's brand intact without alienating its many new members.

"Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" matches the acronym for the body's five original members — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — whilst also denoting goals which the new members — Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates — can get behind.

"It's an elegant way to reinterpret BRICS so that the acronym represents a joint mission rather than country names," Mihaela Papa, director of the BRICS Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, told DW.
For Sushant Singh, lecturer in South Asian Studies at Yale University, the vague slogan reflects India's desire as hosts to keep BRICS as low-key and neutral as possible.
"India doesn't want to offend Russia or China, but the fact is that Indians are looking more towards the United States these days. The desire to build up BRICS is not there."
Why India's role at the BRICS summit matters
Yet host India's status as a rising global geopolitical power has added clout to this year's gathering when compared with last year's summit in Brazil.

At the Rio de Janeiro gathering, six of the bloc's 11 heads of state skipped the event, including major players like Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin is expected to attend, while Xi is widely expected but not yet formally confirmed by Beijing.
"The participation of China's top leadership is crucial," says Papa.
She also thinks it would be a significant sign of the BRICS' strength as a "stabilizing force" if the leaders of regional rivals Iran and the UAE were shown to be able to work together.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will attend but UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is expected to send representatives. Saudi Arabia, another Iranian foe, is also expected to. The country's BRICS status remains somewhat ambiguous, although current official BRICS materials generally list it as a member.

blocks.caption: Several heads of state skipped the 2025 gatheringImage: Fabio Teixeira/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: For India, the summit is as significant for the bilateral meetings it brings as much as for the BRICS gathering itself. Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are due to meet on Friday while the summit will also present an opportunity for Xi and Modi to speak face-to-face amid continued strain in the China-India relationship.
However, that does not mean much of substance will emerge from the weekend.
"In terms of concrete outcomes and what is achievable, I think it's going to be very, very limited," says Singh.

Modi has spoken of BRICS as an important forum for the 'Global South' to present a common front on various issues. He has also spoken about "a people-centric approach" and the spirit of "humanity first".
However, Singh says BRICS is simply not a priority for India and that in general, Delhi has not appreciated what many have interpreted as the "anti-western" turn the group has taken in recent times.
"With India as chair, India won't be comfortable with any kind of anti-western line," he says, pointing to the focus it places on defense ties with the US and trade ties with the West as a whole.

blocks.caption: The leaders of Russia, China and India will all be present this yearImage: REUTERS/ANI

blocks.text: "India's idea of BRICS is more to look at improving trade ties, etc. In other words, can we do things which are beneficial to us without in any way being confrontational or critical of the West?"
Yet ironically, India's non-aligned status means it may actually be able to keep the bloc aligned.

"India adds clout because it has significant geopolitical weight and relationships across competing camps, making it an important bridge-builder," says Papa. "Its approach is likely to keep BRICS focused on practical cooperation and global governance reform rather than overt bloc politics."
What is BRICS for anyway?
BRICS is soon approaching its 18th birthday, so in a sense it should be coming of age. Yet the bloc has struggled for coherence in recent years amid doubt over its purpose.
The scale of what it could represent is not in doubt. It boasts nearly half the world's population among its members and around 40% of its GDP.

Last year, its joint declaration called for reforms of global governance, specifying representation on multilateral bodies such as the IMF and the World Bank. It also condemned tariffs and decried what it called the "polarization" of the international order.
"Ideologically, BRICS remains where it was during the last summit in Brazil, focused on practical, functional cooperation while seeking to avoid geopolitical tensions," says Papa.

blocks.caption: BRICS foreign ministers have already met ahead of the summitImage: ANI

blocks.text: She says that the expansion of the group from five to 11 members — if we include Saudi Arabia — has made it harder to reach consensus on various issues.

There are also now more autocracies among its members than democracies, while many members have tense bilateral relations. "These internal contradictions will always be hard to reconcile," says Singh.
What could the BRICS summit achieve?

Nonetheless, Papa says she expects progress this year in three areas: trade, monetary cooperation, and agriculture. Discussions are likely to focus on improving trade between the members, alternative financial architecture for exchanging currencies and on issues around food security.

While talk of reforming global governance will still be central, she thinks BRICS' best hope to focus on the institutions which it agrees most on. For example, India is reluctant to press for UN reform but is keen for a co-ordinated approach from BRICS to trade and the WTO.
"India's WTO ambitions are shared by more members," she says, which makes movement in that area "more likely."
Yet many still share Singh's view that the group will "continue to underwhelm."
He says issues ranging from China's growing global dominance to the Trump administration's stance on tariffs have made the bloc's limited goals even harder to achieve.
"With the kind of world that we are in and the lack of coherence and internal contradictions that BRICS has, it's very unlikely that it will achieve anything major," he says.

articles.title: MTRCB ready to regulate streaming platforms
articles.summary: MANILA – The Movie and Television Review and Classification Board (MTRCB) said Friday it is ready to regulate streaming platforms such as Netflix, HBO and Disney if Congress expands its…

blocks.text: MANILA – The Movie and Television Review and Classification Board (MTRCB) said Friday it is ready to regulate streaming platforms such as Netflix, HBO and Disney if Congress expands its mandate, while pushing for stronger safeguard against violent content reaching children online.

MTRCB Chair Lala Sotto told the Senate Committee on Finance that the agency can take on subscription video-on-demand and other online streaming services, but stressed that its role should be regulation rather than prior censorship.

“We will accept the challenge if the legislators would include the said online services, streaming platforms, the subscription video on-demand services in our jurisdiction or our purview,” Sotto said during the hearing of the agency’s proposed 2027 budget chaired by Senator Erwin Tulfo.
She said films shown on streaming platforms need not undergo prior review, but providers should establish effective complaint mechanisms and commit to responding when concerns are raised.
“Currently, we are working with Netflix and HBO and Disney and they’ve been very cooperative,” Sotto said.
Tulfo raised concern over children’s easy access to explicit and violent content, including online games and material linked to recent incidents of school violence.
Sotto acknowledged that online games and social media remain outside MTRCB’s present jurisdiction, although the agency has begun studying possible regulatory approaches.

MTRCB Executive Director Roberto Diciembre said one option is a “do not amplify” policy that would require major platforms to prevent algorithms from automatically promoting violent material, especially to minors.
Under such an approach, violent content could be barred from algorithmic recommendations, graphic material age-gated, autoplay disabled, and monetization of violent videos restricted.

“Kung pwede, hindi ma-monetize because sa totoo lang, isa sa mga motivation ng mga content creators, syempre ma-monetize yung gagawin nilang content (If possible, it should not be monetized because, in reality, one of the motivations of content creators is to earn from the content they produce),” Diciembre said.
He said stronger “safety by default” rules could also be imposed for minors, including tighter privacy settings and safeguards against repeated exposure to violent material.
The agency is also studying special emergency protocols for livestreamed violence, particularly during mass shootings, terrorist attacks, hostage situations, riots and similar incidents.

Diciembre said platforms may need rapid escalation mechanisms to immediately route critical issues to government authorities because livestreaming can spread harmful content before ordinary moderation systems can respond.
For now, however, Tulfo noted that MTRCB cannot impose such measures without an expanded mandate from Congress.

“Unless you will be given by Congress and the Senate to expand your powers to look into online platforms, social media, online games. For now, wala kayong magagawa (there is nothing you can do)?” Tulfo asked.
“Yes,” Diciembre replied.

For 2027, MTRCB proposed total spending of about PHP197.9 million, of which PHP53.39 million would come from the national government while PHP144.51 million, or about 73 percent, would be sourced from agency-generated income.
The agency also proposed PHP35.78 million in capital outlay for ICT software and equipment, including the second year of redevelopment of its transaction and collection system. (PNA)

articles.title: Buddhist monk arrested in suspected $3m embezzlement scandal
articles.summary: Thai police also arrested a suspected female accomplice with whom the monk, who had taken a vow of celibacy, was filmed having sex.

blocks.text: Thai police have arrested a Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling 100 million baht ($3m; £2.2m) from his monastery, along with a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.

Phra Wachirayan Wi, a former abbot at the prominent 14th-Century Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, allegedly pocketed donations meant for the temple on more than 20 occasions over two years.
In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions. He was defrocked after his arrest. He has yet to comment publicly.
The latest arrests come just over a year after another sex-and-blackmail case involving senior monks rocked Thailand's monastic community.
The 66-year-old was known for creating a highly-coveted coin amulet. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul reportedly owns some of his creations.
Thailand's Buddhist institution has long been plagued with reports of monks breaking their vow of celibacy, trafficking drugs and committing financial crimes.

In July last year, police opened a hotline for people to report "misbehaving monks" after at least nine monks were found to have had sex with a woman. She then blackmailed them with photos and videos of the acts for nearly $12 million.

Police on Friday said they identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts Phra Wachirayan had issued in the temple's name – one was meant for temple renovations, while the other was payment for amulets and other sacred objects.
"But the money from both streams did not enter the temple's account. Not a single baht," lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan told a news conference, according to reports.

Police found cash and gold bars worth more than 100 million baht while raiding Phra Wachirayan's residence on Thursday, with counting going on until late into the night, Thai news outlet The Nation reported.
While examining CCTV footage in the residence, police found a clip of him having sex with a woman on his dining table.
Authorities identified her as 47-year-old Punyavee Rungrueang, who has been arrested on charges of abetting a state official in illegal activities. She has yet to comment publicly.
Many monks in Thailand receive stipends from the government and are therefore considered state officials.
Police seized 35 gold amulets, along with about 1.5kg of gold bars and jewellery, worth an estimated 6.04 million baht, from Punyavee's home.
Police believe Punyavee helped Phra Wachirayan manage his embezzled proceeds, noting that tens of millions of baht circulated through her bank accounts each year, The Bangkok Post reported.
Investigators say they started looking into the case in mid July, after receiving an anonymous tip alleging Phra Wachirayan of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.
Two or three other people could be involved in the case, they say.

articles.title: Balisacan: 2028 election results crucial to PH economic growth
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The outcome of the 2028 national elections will be crucial to the Philippines’ economic growth, Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev) Secretary Arsenio…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The outcome of the 2028 national elections will be crucial to the Philippines’ economic growth, Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev) Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said.
In a roundtable discussion with INQUIRER reporters and editors on Friday, Balisacan said the next elected president should appoint Cabinet members who are true experts in their respective fields.
This comes as the government tries to keep up with neighboring countries in terms of economic growth, as measured by gross domestic product.

Thailand and Indonesia, for example, were way ahead of the Philippines in 2010, but the Philippines was able to catch up after its economy grew much faster than those of the other two nations, especially Thailand.

“We cannot afford to go back to the old ways. We hope to sustain this growth. Hopefully, as I was saying, the last three quarters and even the whole year this year are transitory, and we will return to a period of higher growth so we will not be left behind by our neighbors,” Balisacan said.
“They’re way ahead. We are trying to catch up faster,” he added.
The Philippine economy in the first quarter of 2026 slowed to 2.8 percent from the 3 percent growth recorded in the last quarter of 2025. It further decelerated to 2.3 percent in the second quarter.
While data for the third quarter is yet to be released, the Asian Development Bank said it expects the Philippine economy to recover in the final two quarters of the year.
Pressure from other countries

Balisacan described as a good kind of pressure the way Filipinos, especially the middle class, are able to compare their way of living in the Philippines with that of other countries whenever they travel.
“I think that Filipinos are very much conscious of their positions relative to our neighbors because of the internet, and so they demand so much from their leaders now,” he said.
“There are pressures, and that pressure’s a good force for us because that could influence the outcome of the electoral process,” he added. /mcm

articles.title: Why North Korea's Kim Jong Un doesn't need a US deal
articles.summary: Donald Trump's overtures to North Korea's dictator have gone nowhere, with an emboldened Pyongyang accelerating its nuclear program and solidifying alliances with Russia and China.

image.caption: Kim's dismissive stance toward Trump reflects North Korea's growing confidence that it no longer needs a grand bargain with the US [FILE: June 30, 2019]Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

blocks.text: Last month, US President Donald Trump revived a charm offensive aimed at Pyongyang by drastically scaling back joint US military exercises with South Korea and pouring praise on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The US president said the North Korean dictator "has always treated me with great respect."

North Korea's response to Trump's overtures has been markedly less enthusiastic, ranging from firing a barrage of missiles to publicly denying Trump's claims that Kim has responded "very positively" to a request for talks.
This week, as the US and South Korea, along with Japan, kicked off a five-day military drill, there was no mention of any pullback from Washington, nor any sign of diplomatic progress with Pyongyang.

Instead, Kim on Monday commissioned a naval destroyer, while again emphasizing North Korea must establish a "powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent" and strengthen "maritime defense." Kim also said North Korea would soon unveil a "significant" naval advancement.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
No urgency for deal with US
Unlike the summit diplomacy of Trump's first term, Kim's dismissive stance comes at a time when North Korea has alternatives to a grand bargain with the United States.

"For Kim, the stakes are simply lower than they were in 2019. There is no longer the same sense of urgency in Pyongyang to get back to the negotiating table with Washington," Joon Ha Park, a correspondent at Korea Risk Group in Seoul, told DW.

"North Korea now has a treaty-based alliance with Moscow and is drawing closer to Beijing, while its military capabilities have expanded significantly. That's why a single reduction in ROK-US military exercises is not enough for Pyongyang to be swayed," he added, referring to military ties between South Korea and the US.
Kim rides high
Park agrees that Kim is arguably in his strongest position since taking power in 2011.

Just six years ago, amid crippling sanctions and the coronavirus pandemic, an emotional Kim stood at the lectern marking the 75th anniversary of the Korean Workers' Party and expressed regret for having failed the North Korean people.

Fast forward to today, and North Korea's economy appears to be on a stronger footing. Estimates released last year by South Korea's central bank showed the economy expanded by 3.7% in 2024, its fastest rate of growth in eight years.
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North

Kim has brought North Korea closer to Russia and China than the traditionally isolated country has been in decades. This week, both Moscow and Beijing sent messages marking North Korea's 78th founding anniversary and praising the strategic importance of their deepening partnerships with Pyongyang.

Kim's recent spate of good fortune began in 2023 after a summit with Vladimir Putin in Russia's far east. The meeting opened the door for North Korea delivering arms to help Russia fight the Ukraine war, with Moscow sending back aid.
Since then, Pyongyang has heavily ramped up industrial military production, buoyed by fresh financing that skirts international sanctions.
Beijing responds to the Russia-North Korea alliance
China, North Korea's traditional benefactor, quickly took notice of the growing alignment between Moscow and Pyongyang, but initially kept its distance.

"The war in Ukraine has opened up a crucial lifeline for the (North Korean) regime, delivering weapons, ammunitions and soldiers to Russia in return for cash, foodstuff and ostensibly advanced military technology," Alexander Lipke, policy fellow with the Asia Program at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"These warming ties with Russia have also alarmed China, which is also actively attempting to cement its position as Pyongyang's preeminent partner," he added.

By 2025, Russia and North Korea's ever closer ties forced Beijing to pivot and showcase its leading role among the three countries. In September that year, Kim was invited to the "Victory Day" celebrations in Beijing, and for the first time, stood publicly on stage alongside Xi and Putin.

For a regime known for its international isolation, Kim standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of Russia and China was a major milestone. This was again the case when in June 2026, Xi's first foreign trip of the year took him to Pyongyang.
Why North Korea is now Europe's problem
Denuclearization off the table?

Notably, any mention of "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" was omitted from communiques following these high-level meetings, despite the phrase previously being part of boilerplate diplomatic language from Beijing and Moscow.

This diplomatic softening comes as North Korea aggressively takes steps to ramp up its nuclear program. In February 2026, Kim said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "irreversible," while calling for the country's nuclear force to be expanded. Recent analysis of satellite imagery suggests increased activity at known North Korean nuclear sites.

Pyongyang has also insisted on US recognition as a nuclear weapons state as a precondition for any talks with Washington, while emphasizing that any future summits must omit language on "denuclearization."

North Korea is estimated to have nearly 60 nuclear warheads, which is double the 20-30 warheads Pyongyang is thought to have possessed during Trump's last diplomatic episode with Kim in 2018 and 2019.

"North Korea is no longer looking for talks centered on denuclearization or even traditional arms control. It increasingly wants recognition, implicitly or otherwise, as a nuclear weapons state," said Park from the Korea Risk Group.

He added that any Trump summit without denuclearization included as part of the official agenda "could be portrayed by Pyongyang both domestically and internationally as implicit US acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status."
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
Sanctions don't matter anymore?

Since its first nuclear test in 2006, North Korea has been subject to a strict sanctions regime, with the UN Security Council having passed nine sanctions resolutions aimed at restricting exports, along with asset freezes.

The last package was passed in 2017. At that point, it was combined with pressure and fiery rhetoric from the first Trump administration, raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula. Kim was under heavy economic pressure and seeking sanctions relief in return for concessions on his nuclear program. But that moment has now long passed.

"North Korea's diplomatic situation has vastly improved, reducing the pressure to come to the table to cut a deal with the US," said Lipke, adding that "independent sanctions enforcement has widely collapsed," with Russia and China no longer actively pursuing their non-proliferation stance of previous decades.
Lipke said North Korea no longer needs a bargain with the US regarding sanctions relief in return for partial denuclearization.

"But the bargain now on the table could potentially be much larger for North Korea, a freeze in nuclear development in exchange for the recognition by the US as a de-facto nuclear state in front of the whole world."

articles.title: ‘Living in Water’ selected for 2026 Aesthetica Film Festival
articles.summary: Produced in partnership with the CMB Foundation-Equity Initiative, the Atlantic Institute, and Rappler, this 360 virtual reality documentary takes viewers to Isla Tibaguin, Bulacan, where flooding is…

blocks.text: Produced in partnership with the CMB Foundation-Equity Initiative, the Atlantic Institute, and Rappler, this 360 virtual reality documentary takes viewers to Isla Tibaguin, Bulacan, where flooding is an ongoing and near-daily occurrence brought by the tides

items: Living in Water, a 360 virtual reality documentary about rising sea levels in the Philippines, has been selected for the 2026 Aesthetica Film Festival, showcasing the struggles of residents in Isla Tibaguin facing daily flooding.
The documentary highlights the impact of climate change on communities, emphasizing the ongoing challenges posed by severe flooding and the inadequacies of government responses to climate risks.

Produced with support from various organizations, Living in Water aims to raise awareness about climate inequity, particularly in countries like the Philippines that contribute least to climate change yet suffer its most severe effects.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Living in Water, a 360 virtual reality documentary about rising sea levels in the Philippines, has been selected for the 2026 Aesthetica Film Festival in York, United Kingdom, which will take place from November 4 to 8, 2026. The documentary will be exhibited along with around 300 short films, games, podcasts, and immersive/VR works.

Aesthetica is one of the United Kingdom’s leading festivals and is a qualifying festival for the British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA) and the British Independent Film Awards (BIFA) in eligible short-film categories.

Living in Water, a 15-minute immersive experience, takes viewers to Isla Tibaguin, Bulacan, Philippines, where flooding is no longer a disaster brought by seasonal typhoons but an ongoing and near-daily occurrence brought by the tides. Residents are forced to conduct the routines of daily life, such as cooking, eating, and walking while submerged in water. The documentary highlights what communities are forced to endure to adapt to the climate emergency.

Living in Water was produced in partnership with the CMB Foundation-Equity Initiative, the Atlantic Institute, and Rappler. The British Council Connections Through Culture Grant also supported the project.

The news of the film’s selection comes as the Philippines continues to experience severe flooding brought by tropical cyclones and an intensified southwest monsoon. Weeks of massive flooding in Metro Manila and surrounding provinces renewed calls for deeper scrutiny of the government’s flood-control infrastructure and climate risk mitigation policies.

When told that Living in Water had been selected for Aesthetica, Riri Sacdalan, one of the main characters in the documentary, told Rappler: “I hope that people who will see the film will understand how difficult life is with flooding that comes almost every day and keeps on getting worse every year. We are used to it but also sick of it. I often wonder if there will ever come a time when our feet can stay dry.”

In recent weeks, the residents of Isla Tibaguin have been contending with worsening flooding and strong monsoon winds. Fisherfolk, including Sacdalan, have not been able to go out to sea, exacerbating pressure on household incomes and food security.

“At the Atlantic Institute, we deeply believe in the potential of VR to communicate the world’s most urgent stories, creating a shortcut from understanding to action. Living in Water exemplifies this potential. We’re delighted to see the film screening at Aesthetica and excited about the impact it can have on audiences, bringing them closer to the realities of the climate emergency,” said Alice Wroe, head of emerging technologies at the Oxford-based Atlantic Institute.

The selection also comes amid destructive climate-related events across Asia. A glacier collapse triggered catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border. In Indonesia, wildfires linked to severe drought brought by a strengthening El Niño are burning through Sumatra and Borneo.

“Living in Water underscores the climate inequity that we are now seeing. Countries that contribute the least to the climate emergency, such as the Philippines, experience its disruption and violence the most. Filmed in 360-degree virtual reality, Living in Water immerses viewers in the daily lives of Riri, Angie, and their community, showing the environmental and human cost of the climate emergency that is unfolding in slow motion,” said Roger Glass, CMB Foundation president and Atlantic Institute board member.

The 2025 World Risk Index ranked the Philippines as the top country with “high exposure to weather-related extremes.” An average of about 20 tropical cyclones enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility each year, with about eight to nine directly crossing the country. Some areas of the Philippines are also experiencing sea level rise that is four to five times faster compared to the global average.

“The climate story is the most important story of our time, and embracing emerging technologies to bring stories like this closer to the audience, especially to those outside the everyday climate reality of Filipinos, has never been more urgent,” said Jee Geronimo, head of environmental reporting at Rappler.
Living in Water will make its large-scale premiere at the Rappler Social Good Summit on November 21, 2026. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Marcos establishes EduPhil program to attract international students
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has issued an executive order establishing the Education Philippines (EduPhil) Program to promote the country as a preferred destination for international…

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 6:31pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has issued an executive order establishing the Education Philippines (EduPhil) Program to promote the country as a preferred destination for international students seeking higher education, research, and training.
Under EO No. 124, the EduPhil Program seeks to facilitate the entry, stay, and education of international students in the Philippines through a whole-of-government framework.

It also aims to support and promote Philippine higher education internationally by advancing academic cooperation, research collaboration, innovation partnerships, knowledge exchange, and global engagement.

“The increasing importance of international education as a driver of economic growth, innovation, cultural diplomacy, human capital development, and international cooperation, together with the rapid evolution of digital governance and regional integration, necessitates a modern, coordinated, and digitally enabled whole-of-government framework to streamline the delivery of government services relating to international education and strengthen the competitiveness of the Philippines as a destination for higher education, research, and academic exchange,” the EO read.

The EO also formed the EduPhil Task Force, which shall serve as the principal inter-agency coordinating body for promoting, facilitating, and developing international students' education in the country.
The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) shall serve as the program's lead implementing agency and the task force's secretariat.
The EduPhil Portal shall also be established to facilitate and streamline the delivery of government services relating to the education of international students in the country.
The initial funding requirement for the program implementation will be charged against the current and available appropriations of the CHED and other concerned agencies.
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto signed the EO on behalf of the President on September 8, 2026. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Meralco rates dip slightly in September despite higher generation costs
articles.summary: For a household consuming 200 kWh, that translates to savings of about P8 on the monthly electricity bill

blocks.text: For a household consuming 200 kWh, that translates to savings of about P8 on the monthly electricity bill
MANILA, Philippines – Meralco customers will see another slight reduction in electricity rates in September, although an increase in generation costs limits the savings for households.

The Manila Electric Company (Meralco) said on Friday, September 11, that its overall rate for a typical residential customer will decline by P0.0409 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), to P14.7424 per kWh from P14.7833 in August.
For a household consuming 200 kWh, that translates to savings of about P8 on the monthly electricity bill.

The decrease came despite the generation charge rising by P0.4232 per kWh, which Meralco attributed mainly to the weaker peso and higher fuel costs amid renewed conflict in the Middle East. (READ: Cheaper PH electricity? Go beyond system loss; fix costly power contracts)

Those increases were more than offset by cheaper ancillary services and lower taxes. Ancillary service charges collected by the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines fell by P0.3344 per kWh as Reserve Market charges declined, while taxes and other charges dropped by a net P0.1657 per kWh.

Meralco said lower taxes were partly due to the completion of the Malampaya gas facility’s maintenance shutdown, allowing First Gas and Prime CoreGen plants to again use more indigenous natural gas, which is exempt from value-added tax. (READ: VAT on system loss may be removed by November – ERC)
The utility is also continuing two previously approved refunds equivalent to a combined P1.0139 per kWh for residential customers. These refunds were already reflected in August bills.
September marks the second consecutive monthly rate reduction after Meralco cut its rate by P0.0428 per kWh in August. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Greens select Zack Polanski to run in Holborn and St Pancras byelection
articles.summary:
Leader has said Greens are underdogs in race for Keir Starmer’s former seat but he is confident they can beat Labour

Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, has been selected as its candidate…

blocks.text: Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, has been selected as its candidate for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October.
The seat became vacant this month when the former prime minister Keir Starmer announced he was leaving parliament.

Polanski has said the Greens, which made gains in the area in the local elections in May, are underdogs in the race but he is confident they can beat Labour, which won the seat with a majority of more than 11,000 at the 2024 general election.

On Wednesday, Labour selected the Camden council leader, Sagal Abdi-Wali, as its candidate. She said: “This place welcomed my family as refugees and gave us hope when we needed it most. I am so grateful to have had the opportunity to build a life here, serving our community as a councillor, school governor and community activist.”

Some in Labour are understood to be concerned about the impact of upcoming oil and gas announcements on the campaign. Industry insiders expect the government to greenlight the Jackdaw gasfield as soon as next week, but there are expectations that any announcement on Rosebank, a contentious oilfield, will be delayed until after the byelection.

Polanski won the race to stand for the Greens over one of the party’s local councillors, Hamza Chowdhury, who had said the constituency did not need “another MP who arrives during an election campaign” and “disappears once the votes are counted”.
At a meeting to announce his candidacy, Polanski said: “The Greens might be the underdog in this election, but we have the momentum, and we can win.

“And it’s clear everyone knows it’s the Green party against Labour, and before May we had one councillor here, and now we have 10. And last weekend we had so many people on the streets that we delivered leaflets to the entire constituency in just a few hours.”

Announcing him as the candidate, Hannah Spencer, the MP for Gorton and Denton, acknowledged that the Labour party has the advantage. She said, “the next few weeks will be tough, of course. Labour have donations from fossil fuel lobbyists and gambling industries, and they have a big machine. But we are powered by people who care, and we have shown that we can beat the establishment parties, the billionaires, and I am living proof of that.”
after newsletter promotion
Polanski said he lived in the constituency when he moved to London 20 years ago and that his barber is still there.

articles.title: Nation pauses to remember September 11 on 25th anniversary | First Thing
articles.summary:
Commemoration ceremonies to be held around the world for the nearly 3,000 killed in 2001 terror attack on US. Plus, JD Vance sets out his stall as heir to Donald Trump

Good morning. It is a…

blocks.text: Good morning. It is a sombre day for the nation as people gather to mourn and remember the nearly 3,000 victims of the attacks on September 11 2001, when 19 al-Qaida hijackers seized control of four airliners, slamming two of the planes into the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth into a field in western Pennsylvania.

We have comprehensive coverage of the anniversary, which will be marked by ceremonies around the world. There are stories of the day from people who were there. Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower, and they spoke to our Washington bureau chief David Smith. Anna Sweeney Rossman was five when her mother, Amy Sweeney, a flight attendant, was killed onboard American Airlines flight 11, and she spoke to Ramon Antonio Vargas about how the events of that day have cast a shadow on her life.

CIA veterans spoke to Robert Tait about the chaos and confusion in the agency as the unprecedented attacks unfolded, and Guardian readers have told us about how September 11 changed their lives. Jason Burke, our international security correspondent, writes that while al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden may have shaken the world on 9/11, it is clear today his wider plans failed.

But we also have to acknowledge that the world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home. This read from David Smith outlines how the day saw heroes emerge showing the best of America, and then the response of US governments left a dark legacy – Guantánamo Bay, the Abu Ghraib scandal – which continues to unfold to this day.

Those who remember September 11 will never forget the haunting images of that day, including the missing people posters that were put up in the confusing aftermath of the collapse of the towers in New York. Captured by the photographer Phil Buehler, they will form part of a new exhibition, and some can be viewed here. As we look back on a day that reshaped our world, our thoughts remain with the victims, their families, and all those whose lives were irrevocably changed 25 years ago.
In other news …

blocks.caption: A person at the Republican national committee midterm convention wears decorative Trump-themed faux currency on his hat. Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

items: Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery.

With his approval rating at a historic low, Trump brought down the curtain on the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention by pleading with supporters to do him “the biggest favor” and “pretend” they are voting for him in November’s US elections.

JD Vance, meanwhile, made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Trump with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success, criticism of the Democrats as “lunatics” and an aggressive dismissal of a protester waving a Mexican flag.

A US appeals court has rejected Trump’s attempt to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting before November’s high-stakes midterm elections, dealing a fresh blow to the president’s attempted crackdown.

Anthropic has detailed efforts by bad actors to misuse its AI for the production of bioweapons. More researchers and staff members at the AI startup have posted their own dire warnings about the safety of the technology, but Elon Musk called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”.

California has adopted what Gavin Newsom described as “nation-leading” legislation that bans addictive social media features for young users, regulates companion chatbots and implements new safeguards around AI.
Sales of previously occupied US homes declined in August to their slowest annual pace in more than a year as home shoppers grappled with rising mortgage rates and home prices.

blocks.caption: Gambian activists Rohey Cham and Sainabou Sey. Photograph: Malick Njie/Reuters

blocks.text: Leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.

blocks.text: Katie Edwards asks the awkward question about Practical Magic 2, would Hollywood have brought the franchise back from the dead if the intervening 28 years looked more visible on Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman?
Don’t miss this: ‘We can’t stop for a second’ – tracking South Korea’s stalkers in real time

blocks.caption: An alert shows on a computer screen. Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The Guardian

blocks.text: Raphael Rashid reports from Seoul on an app that has allowed survivors – who are overwhelmingly women – to see exactly where their stalker is. If they come within a kilometre, an alert is passed to police and probation authorities, who can call and notify the victim.

blocks.caption: Caitlin Cassidy restarts her algorithm. Illustration: Guardian Design

blocks.text: “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days” is a message we have long since stopped seeing on Instagram. In the wake of a government decision to insist companies provide algorithm opt-outs, my Australian colleague Caitlin Cassidy tried to turn her social media experience back to 2012.
Climate check: English winemakers expect ‘vintage year’ after record-breaking summer heat

blocks.caption: A vineyard in West Chiltington, England. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: While drought in France has been bringing predictions of a fall in wine production, English winemakers are benefiting after record-breaking summer heat quickly ripened grapes. It isn’t all good news for British drinkers though – beer sellers have warned of a potential shortage after the high temperatures caused poor yields of barley.
Last Thing: Diana’s ‘revenge dress’, worn when Charles revealed infidelity, up for auction

blocks.caption: Diana wearing her ‘revenge dress’ in 1994. Photograph: Princess Diana Archive/Campbell Addy for Sotheby’s

blocks.text: Worn by Diana the same night Charles would reveal his infidelity on TV, the black, fitted, off-the-shoulder, skintight and short Christina Stambolian dress was quickly labelled “the revenge dress” by the media. This month it will go on display at Sotheby’s auction house in London, before travelling to Hong Kong, Geneva and New York, where it will be sold.

articles.title: Yemen: Houthis tighten control of strategic Red Sea towns
articles.summary: Reports indicate Houthi militants have taken over the port city of Mokha along with Perim Island, which occupies a strategic position on a vital transport waterway in the Red Sea.

image.caption: The port city of Mokha lies near the crucial Bab el-Mandeb strait [FILE: August 10, 2026]Image: Al Joumhouriya TV/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Yemen's Houthi militia have captured strategic points on the Bab el-Mandeb strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes.

In addition to the Iran-backed group's takeover of the port city of Mokha yesterday, Yemeni government sources told several news agencies on Friday that the Houthis have now also captured the island of Perim, also called Mayyun in Arabic.

Reuters reported that Yemeni government forces said they had withdrawn from Perim, and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, located south of Mokha and closer to the narrowest part of the strait.
Mokha is located 80 kilometers up the Red Sea coast from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, while Perim Island is located in the strait itself.
Vital Red Sea transport route vulnerable?
The Red Sea has served as a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted amid the United States' war with Iran, sending global oil prices skyrocketing.

Houthi spokesperson Abdulsalam was cited by the Reuters news agency as saying that freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Strait remain safe and operations are limited to specific targets.
The Houthis have in the past targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, saying it is in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
Meanwhile, Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz.
"The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel was cited by AFP news agency as saying.
Dhubab lies just south of Mokha.

blocks.caption: For a long time, Mokha had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government [FILE: September 2021]Image: Planet Labs Inc./AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting intensifies between Houthis and Yemeni government

Fighting has intensified between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government in recent months after four years of relative calm, with rebels intensifying efforts to solidify their control over the country's coastline.
The capture of Mokha is the Iran-backed militia's biggest territorial gain since a UN-brokered truce signed in 2022.
The Iran-backed Houthis control the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, as well as much of the more populous areas in the country's north and west.
The internationally recognized government has its headquarters in the southern city of Aden and receives considerable support from Saudi Arabia.
Yemen's civil war has killed over 150,000 people and brought others to the brink of famine.

articles.title: Turks in Germany anxious after AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany party's win in Saxony-Anhalt has alarmed people of Turkish origin in eastern states. Will workers and business owners abandon the increasingly AfD-friendly region for the…

image.caption: Ahead of Sunday's election, people of migration background went on a symbolic daylong strike in the eastern state of Saxony-AnhaltImage: Monika Stefanek/DW

blocks.text: The nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's 43.8% share of the vote in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has prompted nationwide alarm. People of Turkish origin are especially worried.

Gökay Sofuoglu, the co-chair of the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), told DW that business owners he has spoken with in Saxony-Anhalt have been especially alarmed. "After the AfD's success, some were thinking of shutting up shop and leaving, first Saxony-Anhalt, then Germany," Sofuoglu said.

He said that initial response was emotional. "We've had a chance to speak to some of them again since," Sofuoglu said. "They're going to wait and see: They're waiting for the formation of a government."
'Problem for Germany'

Sofuoglu said people of Turkish descent in Saxony-Anhalt regard the rise of the AfD "as a problem for Germany as a whole." He said the party's election win was a threat to the stability of democracy in Germany.

blocks.caption: Anti-AfD protests were held across Germany after Sunday's electionImage: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Although the AfD campaigns heavily against migration, Sofuoglu said he believed that the party's true target is Germany's constitution. He said many people of Turkish origin were inclined to see the party's election win as an immediate threat to their communities rather than look at the AfD's wider aims.
"Much as the rise of the AfD affects us, this is a generally anti-democratic development, and we, along with all democratic forces, must act to counter it," he said.

The AfD's victory has also raised concerns about an increase in nationalist violence within Germany. "There's a fear that the coming days could see more attacks like the ones carried out by the National Socialist Underground, and that there will be no clarification of what's behind them," Sofuoglu said, referring a yearslong neo-Nazi terror spree in Germany.
Grasping the root

A feared increase in nationalist violence is only one part of the discussion. "I don't think that just being concerned achieves anything," Alaz Sümer, a lawyer who works with a nongovernmental organization in Berlin, told DW. "You have to think about the causes. I don't think the established parties have sufficiently addressed the problems that allowed the AfD to become so strong."

blocks.caption: According to current polls, 29% of German voters support the AfDImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sümer came to Germany nine years ago to study. He's currently working on a PhD about extreme-right political parties, and advises people from migrant communities on how to get their international qualifications recognized in Germany.
"Saying 'the AfD is bad, the AfD is dangerous' is the easy way," Sümer said. "We already know that."
Win no surprise
Irmak, who asked that her real name not be used, moved to the eastern city of Leipzig to study 12 years ago. She said the AfD's victory was worrying, but not a surprise.

"It was to be predicted that the far right would do well, and would emerge from the election as the strongest party," Irmak said. "But the ground for this result was also prepared by government policies not addressing citizens' needs."

Irmak said the rise of the AfD would not address Germany's structural problems. "Even with a change of government, it won't alter the need for workers and young people," she said, "especially not in a state with an elderly population, like Saxony-Anhalt."
An AfD ban?

Sümer said German authorities would need to be cautious in dealing with the AfD, which he called an extremist party that is now "a reality in Germany." He said banning the AfD, as many have called for, would only make the party stronger.

blocks.caption: Sümer said politicians must try to address the concerns of AfD votersImage: Privat

blocks.text: If the AfD were banned, Sümer said, a new party would be founded, and more extremist members might fall in with less-visible organizations. That would make Germany "even more uninhabitable" for migrants, he said.

Sümer said Germany's other parties should engage with AfD voters to understand their motives. He said the problem of racism in Germany was bigger than just the AfD, and that the issues that migrants face withing the country were not created by to the party.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, Saxony-Anhalt had a population of about 2.1 million people in 2025. Approximately 249,000, or just over 10%, had a migration background; 6,120 were people of Turkish origin. There are roughly 3 million people of Turkish origin in Germany.
This article was originally written in German.
